title: Four Ways to Deploy More Secure AI Agents | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: After six months of red-teaming enterprise AI agents, NVIDIA's AI Red Team reports that the same four failure modes recur regardless of framework: no access control on the agent, tools enabling arbitrary code execution, no network egress controls, and plaintext secrets inside the agent environment. Their central claim is that prompt-based and LLM-as-a-judge defenses are reliably defeated by social engineering, frog-boiling, and misdirection, so controls must be deterministic and enforced outside the model's control plane.

insights.claim: Connecting an LLM to live tools and corporate data through an agentic harness converts a helpful assistant into privileged software with a poorly understood attack surface.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Enterprise agent deployments create a new class of privileged-access risk that current security tooling does not cover — a real addressable market for agent-runtime security products.
insights.quote: connecting a large language model (LLM) to live tools and corporate data through an agentic harness risks turning a helpful assistant into privileged software with a poorly understood attack surface.
insights.locator: Knowledge workers are increasingly integrating

insights.claim: Across six months of assessments spanning simple interactive coding tools to always-on autonomous digital assistants, exploitable agents exhibited the same four failure modes regardless of the framework or harness used.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Framework choice is not a security differentiator — vendors marketing agent frameworks on safety grounds are selling something the red team says does not vary by framework.
insights.locator: Over the past six months, the NVIDIA AI Red Team

insights.claim: Fully autonomous systems holding enterprise credentials are inherently risky and can nearly always be subverted given sufficient time and expertise, even when built on frontier models.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Sets a ceiling on how autonomous enterprise agents can safely become — supports architectures that constrain blast radius rather than those betting on better model alignment.
insights.quote: While frontier models make adversarial manipulation more difficult, with sufficient time and expertise, nearly all of them can still be subverted.
insights.locator: Our AI Red Team’s experience in securing AI agents

themes.theme: Access control as the cheapest defense

insights.claim: The most common failure mode in current AI deployments is a lack of access control to the agent itself, with multiple agents found holding individual users' credentials while being reachable by any authorized user on the internal network.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Agents become credential-aggregation points that turn ordinary internal network access into lateral privilege escalation — an audit item boards should be asking about.
insights.locator: The most common failure mode in current AI deployments

insights.claim: Agents that simply refused to respond to unauthorized users were significantly harder for the red team to test, making basic authentication the highest-return control per unit of effort.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: The cheapest control produces the largest measured attacker friction — a fast, low-cost remediation for any enterprise already running internal agents.
insights.quote: agents that did not respond to unauthorized users were significantly harder to test
insights.locator: Restrict each agent to explicitly authorized users

insights.claim: Agent permissions should be matched to those of the invoking user rather than held as a standing service identity, applying least privilege to the agent's delegated authority.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Implies identity-delegation infrastructure becomes a required layer in agent stacks, expanding the role of IAM vendors into AI runtime.
insights.locator: Match the agent’s permissions to those of the user

themes.theme: Code execution is the dominant risk

insights.claim: Arbitrary code execution should be treated as the single highest-impact risk in an accessible agent, and command-line tools should be avoided wherever possible.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: The generality that makes shell tools attractive to agent builders is precisely what makes deployments exploitable — expect enterprise procurement to start banning unrestricted shell tools.
insights.quote: Treat arbitrary code execution as the single highest-impact risk in an accessible agent.
insights.locator: Treat arbitrary code execution as the single

insights.claim: LLM-as-a-judge command review is structurally predisposed to fail because legitimate development workflows require commands like pytest or npm install, which under attacker-controlled input are equivalent to arbitrary command execution.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Command allowlisting cannot work for coding agents because the allowed commands are themselves execution primitives — a fundamental limit, not a tuning problem.
insights.locator: Many common agentic command-line tasks support

insights.claim: Even without a shell tool, file read and write access lets an attacker achieve code execution by writing to ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, ~/.gitconfig, hooks.json, MCP.json, or skills files that a different process later executes.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Removing the Bash tool is not sufficient hardening; the config-file surface introduced by MCP and skills ecosystems is itself an execution vector.
insights.locator: An attacker who can write content to system files

insights.claim: Writes outside a non-executable workspace should be blocked at the OS level, and any execution tool must run inside an isolated, escape-hardened environment such as Docker, NVIDIA OpenShell, or a virtual machine that cannot rewrite its own configuration.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Sandboxing moves from optional to mandatory in agent architectures — NVIDIA is positioning OpenShell into that requirement, alongside container isolation vendors.
insights.locator: Run arbitrary command execution only in a sandbox

insights.claim: External strings such as filenames and document titles passed through the command line must be sanitized and normalized to prevent path traversal and command injection, reviving classic injection risk inside agentic pipelines.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Decades-old appsec failure modes reappear in agent harnesses, meaning existing secure-coding tooling has a new surface to sell into.
insights.locator: Exercise caution when processing arguments

insights.claim: When network egress controls were enforced and least-privileged, the red team was forced to run all interactions through the agent process itself, slowing their execution pace and making impact less reliable.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Egress control measurably raises attacker cost even when it doesn't prevent compromise — a defensible ROI argument for network-layer controls around agent runtimes.
insights.locator: Deny network egress by default

insights.claim: Injecting secrets as environment variables — standard practice in non-agentic applications — is insecure for agents, because inducing the agent to run env, printenv, or read /proc/self/environ exposes them directly.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: A widely deployed twelve-factor security pattern becomes an anti-pattern under agents, forcing re-architecture of secret delivery across existing CI and container fleets.
insights.quote: While injecting secrets as environment variables is standard in non-agentic applications, this is insecure for workloads that execute arbitrary code.
insights.locator: Do not expose secrets at rest or to the environment

insights.claim: Command-line tools are especially high risk because CLIs cache credentials on disk in predictable locations, with tokens observed in git repositories, .env files, bash history, .netrc files, and OAuth 2.0 refresh tokens.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: The existing developer-tooling ecosystem leaks credentials by design; agent adoption converts that latent exposure into an active exfiltration path.
insights.locator: Command-line tools are worth highlighting

insights.claim: Even with egress controls preventing network exfiltration, the red team extracted credentials through the chat interface itself because the LLM could read them and deliver them conversationally.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: The model's own output channel is an exfiltration path that network controls cannot see — chat-connected agents need output-side data-loss controls too.
insights.locator: Even when we could not establish a reverse shell

insights.claim: Secrets should live in a dedicated secrets manager, be retrieved on demand only into the memory of the process that needs them, and where possible be issued by a token broker as short-lived, narrowly scoped tokens revoked at task completion.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Points to demand growth for ephemeral-credential brokering as a distinct product category alongside classic vaults.
insights.locator: Never make persistent secrets accessible to an agent

insights.claim: Defenses that live in the same control plane as the LLM, particularly prompt-based defenses, are routinely subverted and inherit the same probabilistic, unreliable behavior as the model itself.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Undercuts the value proposition of prompt-layer safety products; the durable spend shifts to deterministic infrastructure controls.
insights.quote: A consistent finding is that defenses in the same control plane as the LLM, particularly prompt-based defenses, are routinely subverted.
insights.locator: Recommended controls

insights.claim: Simply framing the attacker as a debugging or admin user was remarkably effective, with one Slack-connected agent writing and executing a reverse shell on request.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Chat-surface integrations like Slack are the highest-exposure agent deployment pattern in enterprises today.
insights.locator: Social engineering the agent

insights.claim: Frog-boiling (Crescendo) attacks extracted secrets by running legitimate-looking workflows that induce errors, then leading the agent to 'discover' that secrets were the underlying cause and reveal them.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Multi-turn conversation history is itself an attack asset, so per-message filtering and session-stateless review are insufficient defenses.
insights.locator: Boiling the frog

insights.claim: Misdirection via package installation remains extremely effective: asking a coding agent to run pip install git+https://... on a weaponized package looks like a standard request but produces arbitrary code execution during installation.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Software supply chain and agent security converge; blocking arbitrary URL and VCS-based installs by default becomes a baseline enterprise control.
insights.locator: Misdirection through legitimate workflows

insights.claim: Agent memory and AGENT.md files could be directly manipulated using the agent's own file-editing tools to construct persistent 'debugging' and 'authorized user' framings.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Persistent-memory features shipping across agent products create durable, self-reinforcing compromise — a product risk for vendors racing to add memory.
insights.locator: In other cases, it was possible to directly manipulate

insights.claim: Least-privilege should extend to tools, MCPs, and skills, with anything that executes, writes, or reaches the network scrutinized, and volume mounts avoided or scoped so nothing writable is mounted into a later-executed path.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Sets a de facto governance checklist for the fast-growing MCP tool marketplace; expect enterprise buyers to demand per-tool permission attestations.
insights.locator: Least-privilege tools, MCPs, skills, etc.

insights.claim: Recent or frontier models are recommended specifically for LLM-as-a-judge patterns because they can be more robust to adversarial manipulation, even though the pattern itself is judged insufficient.
insights.speaker: Rich Harang
insights.so_what: Security requirements become a recurring upgrade driver for model spend, favoring frontier-model vendors over cheap static open-weight deployments in guard roles.
insights.locator: Use recent/frontier models, particularly for LLM-as-a-judge
